angle: Edgar has always minted a free body for every Vampire you cast; this issue is about the three cards that make that body cost the whole table life the instant it lands — and about racing with them instead of waiting on a deterministic kill you draw one game in twenty.

teases: PURPHOROS, COUNTED: five triggers off one two-mana Vampire — 10 damage to every opponent, checker-cleared
TOKEN INTO DAMAGE: the layer that decides your game, drawn in 43.2% of games at a mean turn of 3.45
THE 4.8% LOTTERY TICKET: two zero-mana table-kills you should almost never play for
NOT A KILL: the end step that drains 14 from every seat and leaves a 15-life opponent alive at exactly 1

departments.headline: TOKENS AS BURN SPELLS
departments.dek: Every Vampire you cast is two bodies before it does anything else. Three cards decide whether that second body is a chump blocker or a burn spell aimed at all three seats — and which one you find first is the game.

callouts.title: CAST CHEAP, CAST TWICE
callouts.text: Nine one-drops and seventeen two-drops. Eminence pays per cast, not per mana, so two small Vampires beat one expensive one on almost every turn you have the choice.

callouts.title: LAY THE PAYOFF EARLY
callouts.text: Impact Tremors on turn two with one body is one damage and reads as durdle. Nobody spends removal on it. That is exactly why it goes down before the thing that makes it lethal.

callouts.title: MULTIPLY LAST
callouts.text: Anointed Procession and Elspeth, Storm Slayer are what turn a two-drop into a kill. Deploy them onto a board that already converts, on a turn you can also cast the Vampire.

captions.Impact Tremors: **THE TWO-MANA DOOR:** one damage to each opponent every time a creature you control enters — and an eminence token is a creature entering, on your turn or anyone else's.
captions.Anointed Procession: **ONE BECOMES TWO:** a replacement effect, so a second doubler makes four. Stack 002 verified the arithmetic and that the order you apply them in never changes the answer.
captions.Purphoros, God of the Forge: **THE CEILING, COUNTED:** four token entries plus the spell's own body is five triggers at 2 damage each — 10 to every opponent from one two-mana Vampire (stack 008).

pilot_tips.text: Resolve Warleader's Call before the wide turn, not after — the +1/+1 is permanent, but the damage only counts creatures that enter once it is already on the battlefield.
Deploy Charismatic Conqueror into a developing table: every artifact or creature an opponent plays untapped either comes in tapped or hands you a lifelink Vampire on their turn.

departments.pull_quote: Your board does not have to survive to a combat step. It only has to enter.

departments.headline: NEVER KEEP FOR EDGAR
departments.dek: He is face up in the command zone before your first decision, so an opener never needs him. The simulation keeps 81.7% of first sevens at 0.214 mulligans a game — the Coach grades four of them and overrules the machine once.

hands.why: Three lands that can all come in untapped, two one-mana Vampires worth two bodies each, a lord, and the two-mana payoff that turns the whole thing into damage. This is the enabler-heavy shape the drill is looking for — a lord or anthem finds you in 82.9% of games anyway.

Two lands reads risky until you price the mana: Ancient Tomb into Sol Ring is three available mana on turn one, and Herald's Horn rebates a mana off every Vampire behind it. Both lands enter untapped, which is the detail that saves this keep.

Half a deterministic kill and four five-drops. Two of those lands enter tapped no matter what you do, nothing happens before turn five, and the eminence dividend for four whole turns is zero. Ship anything whose cheapest spell costs four.

hands.verdict: SHIP — the hand the machine keeps
hands.why: The simulation's rule keeps two to five lands, so this five-lander passes it — and the Coach ships it anyway. One castable spell before turn four, and protection plus a tutor are luxuries in an opener rather than a plan. The badges disagreeing in public is the honest version of this section.

captions.Concealed Courtyard: **THE FIRST-THREE-TURNS LAND:** untapped exactly while nine one-drops and seventeen two-drops need it. Sixteen of the 37 lands can enter tapped; only three of them always do.

pilot_tips.text: Grade a one-drop by casts, not by stats — Viscera Seer on turn one is a body, a banked eminence token, and a scry every time something of yours dies.

departments.pull_quote: He lives in the command zone. Mulligan like he does not exist.

departments.headline: COMMIT BEFORE WE DO
departments.dek: Two boards where the comfortable instinct is the losing one. Read the branches, say your answer out loud, and only then look at the verdict.

callouts.title: COUNT THE OPEN MANA FIRST
callouts.text: Before you present anything that ends the game, count every untapped source at the table. A held answer appears the moment you commit and never the turn before.

callouts.title: SEQUENCE BY WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE
callouts.text: The enchantment that reads as durdle goes down first; the 5/5 flying deathtouch Vampire goes down last. You are not hiding a plan, you are choosing which piece eats the removal.

captions.Flawless Maneuver: **FREE, CONDITIONALLY:** it costs nothing while you control your commander — which is an argument for casting Edgar on the turn you intend to overcommit, not for casting him early.

pilot_tips.text: Spend Teferi's Protection on the turn you commit the board, not the turn you fear the wrath — it answers the sweeper and the swing-back with one card.

departments.pull_quote: The window is not the turn you can win. It is the turn they cannot answer.
departments.note: EDITOR FLAG: decisions/002-vito-tutor-or-hold.json still describes a board containing Black Market Connections and Nighthawk Scavenger and a branch that tutors for Exquisite Blood — none of which is in this 99. The renderer prints decision scenarios verbatim and validate-issue does not check decision card names, so this spread will ship a board the reader cannot build. It needs regenerating against the current list before the issue is rendered; nothing in this plan's copy depends on it. Decision 001 (cast Edgar or keep casting) is clean and is the spread this section's copy is written around.

departments.headline: THE TURN THEY TURN ON YOU
departments.dek: Nobody fears a board of 1/1s. They fear the trigger that makes those 1/1s hit all three of them at once — and you get to choose which turn that is.

callouts.title: THE THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: You become the archenemy the first time a token entering the battlefield deals damage at every seat. Before that trigger you are a fair creature deck. After it, no combat step is required and the whole table knows it.

callouts.title: PAYOFFS EARLY, MULTIPLIERS LATE
callouts.text: Impact Tremors on turn two is one damage and reads as nothing. Elspeth, Storm Slayer is a five-mana planeswalker at an aggro table and gets attacked on sight. Deploy in that order every time.

callouts.title: NAME THE SEAT THAT CAN SWITCH YOU OFF
callouts.text: Your exposure is not the wrath. It is broad exile or artifact-and-enchantment removal. Track which player holds it and treat them as the one who can turn the machine off.

captions.Sanguine Bond: **THE CARD THAT ANNOUNCES ITSELF:** five mana, no body, no creature type. Every other piece of the deterministic kill pays rent as a Vampire; this one tells the table exactly what you are holding.
captions.Elspeth, Storm Slayer: **LAST, ALWAYS:** she doubles every token you make, and she is a planeswalker in a room full of attackers. She goes onto a board that already converts, never onto an empty one.

pilot_tips.text: Cast Bloodthirsty Conqueror as a 5/5 flying deathtouch body whenever you do not hold the other half — a card paying full rent tells the table nothing at all.

departments.pull_quote: A wrath is a bad card against you. Say so out loud — it is true, and true table talk is the only kind that keeps working.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: It is not the sweeper and it is certainly not the graveyard hate. Find the seat holding broad enchantment removal, because that is the only player at the table who can switch the machine off.

threats.read: The wrath is a worse card against you than against anyone else at the table, and you should build the whole matchup on that. Anointed Procession, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Caretaker's Talent, Patchwork Banner, Legion's Landing and Elspeth all live through it; Purphoros is indestructible and, at this deck's usual devotion, not even a creature. Eminence rebuilds at one token per Vampire cast with no card spent and no tax. So commit exactly the width that converts now and keep the next multiplier in hand. A protection piece is held in 68.0% of games, 56.6% by turn six.

Structurally your best matchup, and the reason is a rules detail worth knowing cold. Eminence is a triggered ability that works from the command zone, not a cast — a Sphere effect taxes the Vampire spell and never touches the token it makes. Nine one-drops and seventeen two-drops keep paying under the tax. Edgar at six mana is the first thing priced out and you do not need him on the battlefield, so leave him zoned longest here and aim Despark at the tax rather than the trophy.

Re-ask the role and take the other seat: against a faster board you are the control, without changing a card. Twenty-nine creatures, lifelink tokens off Charismatic Conqueror and Legion's Landing, deathtouch on Vampire of the Dire Moon and Preacher of the Schism, first strike from Edgar, Cemetery Gatekeeper and everything Stromkirk Captain touches. A wide board turns their small creatures into dead cards without you drawing anything. Track each opponent's clock separately — 40 life attacked from three directions is not 40 life.

You are the clock and you are fast enough to be one: the lord package assembles at a mean turn of 2.58 and the conversion layer at 3.45. Held answers rot here, so spend the exile removal on the piece that ends the game rather than the piece that looks scary. Present the plan that survives being answered — a countered multiplier costs a card, an interrupted alpha strike costs the board. Do not steer toward the deterministic kill in this matchup: it is drawn in 4.8% of games and one instant-speed removal spell breaks it at any iteration.

This one is close to free and you should encourage it. There is no graveyard plan to attack — the kills are token entries, attack triggers and a lifegain loop, and every payoff is a permanent on the battlefield. A Rest in Peace effect costs the reanimator seat their whole deck and costs you one Cemetery Gatekeeper trigger. Say yes to that trade every time and help the hate resolve. Kalitas is your own flip card: their nontoken creatures get exiled instead of dying and you get a 2/2 for each.

pilot_tips.text: Against a 'players can't gain life' effect, keep casting — Purphoros deals damage and Sanctum Seeker's half of the trade is life loss; only the Conqueror pairings notice the hate at all.
Count your non-Vampires before you cast Olivia's Wrath — Mondrak, Abzan Falconer, Ocelot Pride and Elspeth's Soldiers die alongside everyone else's board.

departments.pull_quote: There is no graveyard to attack. Help the hate resolve, and thank them for it.
departments.note: Every card named in an 'outs' list is in the 99 — checked against cards.json. Threat rates are ★ judgment and are ordered by how much the matchup actually costs this list: combat-oriented decks and stax read low because the engine is noncreature and command-zone-fed; faster combo reads highest because the deck's answer to it is speed, not interaction.

departments.headline: BUY THE RACE, NOT THE LOOP
departments.dek: Counted as wildcards, your three tutors take the conversion layer from 43.2% to 67.7% and the deterministic kill from 4.8% to 24.0%. Only one of those numbers is worth spending a card on.

captions.Vampiric Tutor: **TOP, NOT HAND:** it buys the answer to a threat you predicted and never one you are watching resolve. Cast it in the end step of the player before you, untap, and draw it.
captions.Diabolic Intent: **THE COST IS FREE:** eminence prints the body you sacrifice. The one time Intent is the wrong tutor is the one time it looks tempting — when your only creature is the blocker keeping you alive.

pilot_tips.text: Ask which missing piece turns your board into damage at three seats this turn, never which card is best — mean available mana is 4.022 on turn four, so Tutor plus a two-drop is one real turn.

departments.pull_quote: A tutor is a copy of a card. It is never a copy of a class.

departments.headline: THE ENGINE NEVER LEAVES
departments.dek: Edgar does not have to be on the battlefield to be working. Once you believe that, half of this deck's hardest decisions stop being decisions.
departments.body:
Start with the question the ladder beside this paragraph is really asking: what does it cost this deck when Edgar Markov dies? The answer is unusual, and it is the reason you may play him the way you do.

Eminence is a triggered ability that functions from the command zone, because the ability itself says which zones it works in — CR 113.6b, and stack 002 put it on the record. Your commander is the only card you are guaranteed to have access to (CR 903.4). In most decks that guarantee is a finisher. Here it is the engine, and it is running from turn one whether or not you ever pay six mana.

So read the tax ladder as a price you are usually right to refuse. The printed cost is {3}{R}{W}{B}; a second cast adds {2}, a third adds {2} again (CR 903.8). The simulation puts him at a median cast turn of six and never reaches a mean of eight available mana inside ten turns — 7.258 on turn ten is as high as it gets. A second Edgar is a whole turn you paid for. A third is a fantasy. Which reframes the protection question: your insurance is not covering an engine, it is covering one alpha strike.

Colour identity is what a Mardu commander charges you (CR 903.4). Three colours of Vampire — every lord, every drain, every entry-damage enchantment — and no green ramp and no blue counterspell for the life of the deck. That is why the ramp here is seven copies of rocks and rebates rather than a stack of land tutors, and why your answers are white exile and black sweepers.

Now the clock nobody at this table is on. Twenty-one commander damage (CR 903.10a) asks for six connections from a 4/4, and this deck does not attack with Edgar six times. Commander damage is a coincidence here, not a plan — his attack trigger, a +1/+1 counter on each Vampire you control, is worth more in one swing than his own damage is all game.

And the political read, which starts before you draw a card. The table sees a Vampire commander and prices you as a creature deck. They are wrong in the direction that helps you: the machine is made of enchantments, and eminence rebuilds the bodies for free. Let them hold the wrath. Cast the second Vampire.

captions.Flawless Maneuver: **INSURANCE, PRICED:** free while you control your commander, so the protection suite gets cheaper on exactly the turn Edgar is exposed — the one turn he is on the battlefield.

pilot_tips.text: Equip the boots on the turn you attack, not the turn Edgar resolves — hexproof does nothing against a wrath, and the recast is {2} more than the first one.

departments.pull_quote: The only card you always have is the one you can most afford to leave where it is.

departments.headline: EVERY CAST COUNTS TWICE
departments.dek: Sixty-three spells with one hidden common cost: every Vampire among them also prints a body from the command zone. The conversion layer leads, because it is the difference between a board and a clock.

roster.role: The conversion layer: entries become damage

cards: Legion's Landing // Adanto, the First Fort

roster.role: Lords, anthems and the alpha strike
The deterministic kill, and its rent
cards: Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose
Midgar, City of Mako // Reactor Raid

captions.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: **THE PATCH:** black carries 39 of the deck's 73 pips on 22 land sources. With Urborg out, every land you control is a Swamp and the whole base pays the short colour.
captions.Bontu's Monument: **RENT ON THE CAST, NOT THE ENTRY:** it discounts your black creatures and drains each opponent when you cast one — the only payoff in the 99 that fires before the body exists.
captions.Abzan Falconer: **COUNTERS INTO EVASION:** Edgar's attack trigger puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire you control, and Falconer gives flying to every creature carrying one.

pilot_tips.text: Cordial Vampire turns every death into an anthem — pay Diabolic Intent's sacrifice with a spare token and the whole board gets permanently bigger for free.

departments.pull_quote: Twenty-nine bodies, three ways to charge for them, and an engine no wrath can reach.
departments.note: Rank is the point: the conversion layer leads because it is what this issue is about, and the manabase closes. Card blurbs render from manual_prose.card_roles; the remaining lands fall into the Depth group. The 30-card box renders as its own labeled strip and points at The Short List for the rulings. Role coverage is 100% with no unclassified cards, so every tile carries a chip. No synergy-graph claim appears anywhere in this issue: 32 edges fall inside this deck, but the graph is a top-10 global shortlist over every tagged card in the format, not a per-deck fit score.

departments.headline: BUY THE RATE, NOT THE CARD
departments.dek: One question prices every entry on this list: how often does a token entering the battlefield cost the table life? Today, 43.2% of games — and roughly two in three reach turn six with the conversion layer still in the library.

callouts.title: THE BODIES ARE NOT THE CONSTRAINT
callouts.text: A multiplier or extra token-maker shows up in 79.0% of games and a lord in 82.9%, both before turn three on average. The thing that turns those bodies into damage shows up in 43.2%. Spend there.

callouts.title: THE BRACKET DOES NOT MOVE
callouts.text: The floor is 4 and four Game Changers set it — Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Teferi's Protection, Vampiric Tutor — independently of any combo content. Nothing on this list changes the tier, and nothing on it was chosen to.

callouts.title: THE CURRENCY IS THE ANSWER SLOTS
callouts.text: Interaction counts 12 copies against an aggro template's five or six. Read the cards and the real answer count is nearer seven — so the list is spending two answer slots and seven cards that serve neither the width plan nor a verified line.

captions.Night's Whisper: **THE SHAPE SWAP:** two cards once, for two life. The counted card-advantage axis reads 4 against a target of 10, and the audit itself names six more draw functions sitting on cards it classifies elsewhere.
captions.Nomad Outpost: **THE UNCONDITIONAL TAPLAND:** one of only three lands here that always enter tapped, in a deck whose modal mana value is 3 and whose short colour is black.

pilot_tips.text: Forerunner searches a Vampire onto the TOP of your library, so it replaces your draw instead of adding to it — sleeve it for the pods slow enough that you can afford to skip a card.

departments.pull_quote: Ten cards. Six are orders, four are already in the box.

departments.headline: BEST IN THE COLOUR YOU NEED LEAST
departments.dek: Black carries 53.4% of your pips on 41.5% of your sources; white carries the lightest bill and always shows up. Here is exactly what that skew costs you on turn two.

captions.Caves of Koilos: **PAY THE LIFE:** from lands alone black arrives on curve 63.9% of the time against white's 83.1%. The painlands and the fetches are how you close that gap, and the drains are how you pay for them.

pilot_tips.text: Prioritise Patchwork Banner over the other rocks — it is the only one that fixes the short colour and pumps the whole tribe in the same slot.

departments.pull_quote: Thirty-six black sources in a 37-land deck is arithmetic that does not exist. Read the gap as posture, not as a defect.
departments.note: Section renders from mana_analysis.json; Ledger's mana_base prose narrates it. Two facts worth keeping visible in the furniture: nothing in this deck produces restricted mana, so every source can pay for an activated ability, and 16 of the 37 lands can enter tapped while only three always do. The renderer emits the declared full-bleed art break immediately after this section.

departments.headline: NINE TARGETS, NO AVERAGE
departments.dek: Ten thousand seeded games, and deliberately no single kill rate. Every target below is measured on its own, because averaging several independent kills would invent a number the simulation never produced.

callouts.title: READ THE MEAN TURN, NOT ONLY THE RATE
callouts.text: A lord or anthem lands at a mean turn of 2.58 and the conversion layer at 3.45. The gap between those two numbers is precisely the stretch of the game where your board looks harmless.

callouts.title: WHY THERE IS NO KILL RATE
callouts.text: Each target is an AND of ORs, evaluated on its own terms. The model cannot express the union of several independent kills, so a deck with more than one has no single assembled figure — and we are not going to average one for you.

callouts.title: ONE CARD IS 7.1% OF AN OPENER
callouts.text: Two of these targets rest on a single named card. That is a ceiling on those lines rather than a defect in the simulation: 4.8% is simply what one card in a singleton deck looks like.

captions.Herald's Horn: **THE CURVE TAX, REBATED:** mean available mana is 2.149 on turn two and 3.176 on turn three against a modal mana value of 3 — a rebate on every Vampire buys more here than another rock would.
captions.Sol Ring: **SPEED, NEVER COLOUR:** it moves the mana curve and leaves the 63.9% on-curve figure for black exactly where it was.

departments.pull_quote: Bodies: 1.75 by turn three, 4.12 by turn six, 6.52 by turn ten. The bodies were never the problem.
departments.note: Every figure quoted anywhere in this issue traces to goldfish_metrics.json at seed 42, 10,000 iterations, max turn 10, against the stamped decklist hash. Per the artifact's own note, target assembly counts cards DRAWN by a turn and the assisted figures model the three unrestricted tutors as wildcards; the unassisted number is the headline everywhere in this issue and the assisted one is always labelled as such.

departments.headline: SIX LINES, ONE NOT A KILL
departments.dek: Six resolutions cleared the checker, and the most instructive of them fails to end the game. An opponent at 15 survives the end step at exactly 1 — printed at full size, because that is the house style.

callouts.title: WHAT THE CHECK MARK MEANS
callouts.text: Every step in every file below cites the Comprehensive Rules, and an adversarial checker read each citation against the full rule text. Where the record is silent, this section says the record is silent.

callouts.title: THE TWO THAT ACTUALLY END IT
callouts.text: Bloodthirsty Conqueror with Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose, and Bloodthirsty Conqueror with Sanguine Bond. Both deterministic, both at zero mana needed, and both broken by one instant-speed removal spell in any iteration's priority window.

callouts.title: THE ONE YOU WILL USE MOST
callouts.text: Stack 008 is not a combo. It is a count: four token entries plus the cast body is five triggers, and 10 damage to every opponent from a two-mana Vampire. That line is available in almost every game the loop is not.

captions.Bloodletter of Aclazotz: **THE WORD IS INSTEAD:** that makes it a replacement effect, applied once per loss event rather than once per turn — so seven attack triggers get doubled seven separate times.
captions.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: **REACH, NOT LETHAL:** seven tapped creatures drain 14 from each opponent at your end step, and a seat at 15 is left alive at exactly 1. The game continues, and the file says so.
captions.Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose: **THE HALF THAT PAYS RENT:** three mana, a Vampire body, a lord target and lifelink for the swarm on demand. The loop is the bonus, not the reason he is in the 99.

departments.pull_quote: A database calls it an infinite. The record calls it deterministic — and then tells you exactly where it breaks.
departments.note: Six checker-passed, presentable stacks render here: 002, 003, 004, 006, 007, 008. manual_prose.combo_lines carries an intro for exactly those six. No copy anywhere in this issue references any other case number, and nothing outside those six is stated as fact.

departments.headline: READ IT TWICE
departments.dek: Six case files, every citation verbatim, nothing paraphrased or summarised. If a claim in this issue wears a check mark, its complete record is sitting right here.
departments.pull_quote: Where the record is silent, the record says so.
departments.note: Renderer-generated from the checker-passed artifacts; the plan supplies packaging only. The two partial findings are the ones worth the reader's time — stack 007's bounded end step, and stacks 004 and 006 each naming the removal window that breaks the loop.

departments.headline: NINETY-TWO HANDS
departments.dek: Ninety-two artists split 127 cards and nobody holds more than four. There is no house style in this collection — so the feature goes to the hand that painted the card this issue is about.

featured.note:
Two cards out of 127, and one of them is the entire thesis. Eric Deschamps painted Purphoros, God of the Forge — the god who turns a creature entering the battlefield into 2 damage at every seat, and the card stack 008 counted trigger by trigger. He also painted Captivating Vampire, the lord that taps five untapped Vampires and takes something of theirs. A payoff and a lord: the two halves of what this deck does, from one hand.

Two of 127 is not a claim of dominance and we are not making one. The census reads as breadth, and the numbers say so plainly: ninety-two artists, 127 cards counted, and the leaders hold four apiece. Fifty-nine sets contribute; the largest single set gives twelve cards by twelve different artists, and the analysis found no contiguous collector-number runs anywhere in the collection.

Nobody bought this deck whole. It was assembled a card at a time across a decade of printings, and a credits page with ninety-two names on it is exactly what that looks like.

also_worth_noting.note: Four cards, three of them lands — Castle Locthwain, Luxury Suite, Savai Triome. The fourth is Throne of the God-Pharaoh, the end-step drain the checker bounded in stack 007. The manabase's house painter, holding one artifact.
The other leader at four: Arcane Signet and Diabolic Intent in the 99, Akroma's Memorial and Leering Onlooker in the box. Two shelves, one hand.
Three cards, all in the 99, all nocturnes — Blood Crypt, Silent Clearing, Twilight Prophet. The closest this collection comes to a mood board.
Three cards, one of them Mondrak, Glory Dominus — the doubler that appears inside two verified files, stacks 002 and 008.
Three cards and four copies: Arid Mesa, Vampiric Tutor, and a Vampire Nocturnus that appears twice. Counted once, because authorship is per card and not per copy.
Three entries and two cards: Strefan, Maurer Progenitor sleeved and again in the box, plus Vampire Gourmand. The count is honest about printings, and we are honest about the count.

captions.Captivating Vampire: **THE OTHER DESCHAMPS:** a lord whose second ability is a removal spell you already paid for — tap five untapped Vampires and their best creature becomes one of yours.

departments.pull_quote: We count cards, not copies. Four Swamps are one credit.
departments.note: artist-credits reports standout: null with the lead artists at four cards, and its own note says to tell a breadth story — so the feature is an editorial pick, chosen for the story, with every count recomputed by the renderer. Scope for the Art File box: the census covers the pilot's whole collection, the 99 plus the 30-card box, 127 cards and 132 copies across 92 artists. Respect the per-entry notes verbatim: Swamp is one card and four copies, Unholy Officiant and Vampire Nocturnus one card and two copies each. drop_runs is empty, so no bought-whole caveat applies and none is implied. Remaining Art File facts: 1 borderless, 0 foil, 20 legendary frames, 9 showcase.

Next issue verbatim from issue.json ('TO BE ANNOUNCED'). Colophon: volume, issue date, deck name, six verified lines, rules version from the case files, decklist sha. Then the deck dossier link and the Fan Content Policy line.

rhythm_notes: The five acts run as specified and the depth ramp is monotonic. Act I opens high (The Game Plan, narrative) and steps down through practice into participation; Act II sits at medium the whole way — reflection, reference, instruction — so the reader is never asked to concentrate twice in a row. Act III drops to browsing for The 99 and imagination for The Short List, which is the deliberate trough before the two dense analysis spreads. Sources Say into By the Numbers is the one genuine dense adjacency in the book and it is covered by the declared breather: the renderer emits the full-bleed commander art break between them, so the reader gets a page with one line on it before the second table. The Kill is the peak, and it is placed after By the Numbers precisely because it reads as narrative — six stories carrying technical content. The appendix descends: deep reference (Judge's Desk, opt-in and collapsed by default), appreciation (Featured Artist), closure. Three additional breathers are built into the copy rather than the structure: the pull quote in The 99, the art-heavy artist gallery, and the graveyard-hate threat box, which is the shortest and funniest thing in Act II on purpose.
gaps: decisions/002-vito-tutor-or-hold.json is stale and will render a board the reader cannot build: it names Black Market Connections and Nighthawk Scavenger on the battlefield and its first branch tutors for Exquisite Blood. None of the three is in this 99. validate-issue does not check decision card names, so this passes form and fails truth. Regenerate the decision against the current list before rendering — a natural replacement question is 'a payoff has resolved and you hold a multiplier: deploy it now into two open blue mana, or cast two more Vampires?', which is where the deck's real pivot lives.

No verified line exists for the deck's actual kill. Stacks 002, 003, 007 and 008 measure tokens per cast, drain per attack, drain per end step and damage per cast; none of them is a scenario in which the deck wins the game. The two candidates worth a resolve-stack run are the three-doubler stack (1->2->4->8 through Anointed Procession, Mondrak and Elspeth as one entry event) and the composition of all three entry-damage payoffs across a single token wave, which the strategic frame prices at 5 x (2+1+1) to each opponent and explicitly does not claim.

Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubling the ENTRY damage — not just the Throne drain — is unverified and would be the single most valuable new file in the book. Stack 007 verified the doubling for one loss source; the frame reasons by analogy to the entry triggers and stops there. Until it is resolved, no copy in this issue claims it, and the pilot should not sequence around it.

Abzan Falconer plus Edgar's attack trigger is an unresolved timing question with real table consequences: whether counters from a declare-attackers trigger are visible to Falconer's static ability before blockers are declared. It is flagged in the frame as needing a scenario and is written here only as what each card says, never as an outcome.

Strategy-DB gaps the frame names and this issue felt: there is no section on token doubling as a multiplicative rather than additive resource, and none on converting board width into non-combat damage. That second one is the whole deck — the corpus can only reach it through a burn-deck frame (philosophy-of-fire) and one clause of multiplayer.asymmetry. A section on trigger-based kills versus combat kills, covering sweeper exposure, the irrelevance of evasion and the fact that the payoff is a noncreature permanent, would be load-bearing for every token deck the magazine ever covers.

The interaction axis reads 12 against an aggro band of 5-6, but three of those copies are Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call and Purphoros carrying removal:damage tags — the token plan counted as answers. The Short List's own gaps note says the real answer count is about seven. Nothing in this issue quotes the 12 as an answer count; if the taxonomy is ever tightened, the axis reading and the prose that leans on it should be re-checked together.

Featured Artist has no standout by construction (lead artists at four cards of 127) so the pick is editorial and labelled as such. If a future pass wants a different lead, Volkan Baǵa painted both Edgar Markov and Sanctum Seeker, which is the commander-first version of the same breadth story.
